title: A Benchmark for Math Misconceptions: Bridging Gaps in Middle School Algebra with AI-Supported Instruction
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of helping AI systems and educators identify students’ algebra misconceptions and common errors more accurately. The authors argue that existing educational AI tools often lack grounding in real classroom misconceptions and that better benchmarks are needed to support diagnosis and targeted instruction. To address this, they build a benchmark of 55 algebra misconceptions/common errors with 220 diagnostic examples drawn from 145 peer-reviewed sources.

The study evaluates the benchmark with GPT-4-turbo using in-context learning. Two experiments were run: one with randomly sampled misconceptions across the whole dataset and one constrained within topic, showing better performance under topic-constrained testing. The authors also conducted a small educator survey and structured interviews with five middle school algebra teachers, four of whom participated in interviews, to assess clarity, classroom relevance, and potential AI uses. Teachers generally recognized the misconceptions as real classroom phenomena and expressed interest in using the dataset with AI for diagnosis and teacher support.

The population context is middle school algebra, especially grades 6–8, although the benchmark itself includes misconceptions relevant to 4th–8th grade algebra-related learning. The educators worked in U.S. public schools, including schools serving underserved populations and one youth correctional facility. The main conclusion is that GPT-4-turbo can identify misconceptions moderately well, especially when constrained by topic and supplemented by educator feedback, but performance varies substantially by topic and is weakest for ratios and proportional thinking. The paper concludes that topic-aware benchmarks, multimodal inputs, and human expertise are important for practical AI-supported misconception diagnosis.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed-style empirical benchmark/evaluation study, but it is not a controlled student learning trial and does not test causal impact on learner outcomes. Evidence is based on model classification performance plus small educator feedback, so it meets only limited credibility criteria for educational effectiveness evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially useful AI support for diagnosing algebra misconceptions, but it does not measure student learning gains or classroom impact. The reported gains are on model diagnostic accuracy rather than direct K-12 educational outcomes, so real-world impact remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: Using GPT-4-turbo as an AI-supported diagnostic assistant to identify middle school algebra misconceptions from student question/answer pairs, with topic-constrained prompting and educator feedback.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates GPT-4-turbo on diagnosing 55 algebra misconceptions across 220 diagnostic examples. In repeated subsampling, performance was 0.526 precision / 0.529 recall when testing across the full dataset, improving to 0.753 precision / 0.748 recall when train/test examples were constrained by topic; with expert relabeling, topic-constrained accuracy reached 83.91% (1,100 iterations).
finding.measure: Precision, recall, and expert-reviewed classification accuracy for misconception diagnosis
